slides.title: Metric Products of Subspaces
slides.notes: Open by positioning Chapter 3 as the metric upgrade to the outer product. Students already know how to span a blade; now the central question is how two spans compare in size, attitude, perpendicular complement, and computational usefulness.

slides.title: Route Through The Metric Layer
slides.notes: Use this slide as the lecture map. The outer product gives subspaces without measurement, the scalar product compares blades of the same grade, contraction handles unequal grades, and the projection, rejection, and reciprocal-frame formulas are applications of the same metric machinery.

slides.title: Blade Scalar Products Read A Gram Matrix
slides.notes: Emphasize that the determinant is not a coordinate trick. It is the compact record of all pairwise vector dot products between two spanning lists, so dependence, orientation, and metric size all show up in one comparison.

slides.title: Angles Between Subspaces
slides.notes: Present the angle formula as a normalized blade comparison. For lines it reduces to the ordinary dot-product angle; for planes it asks how much oriented area in one plane matches oriented area in the other, with degeneracy detected by a vanishing norm.

slides.title: Contraction Lowers Grade
slides.notes: Slow down on the intuition. A contraction is not simply projection and it is not another outer product. It tests one blade against another with the metric, then returns the lower-grade piece that remains with orientation still attached.

slides.title: Projection And Rejection
slides.notes: Connect the formula to the diagram. The contraction produces a plane-oriented in-span object, multiplication by the blade inverse converts it back to a vector, and the rejection is the residual whose dot products with the spanning directions should vanish.

slides.title: Direct Blades And Dual Constraints
slides.notes: Use direct and dual descriptions as two legitimate views of the same subspace. The direct blade lists directions that span the object, while the dual uses the ambient pseudoscalar and metric to encode the perpendicular constraint.

slides.title: Inner Product Diagnostics
slides.notes: This is the troubleshooting slide. Before trusting a number, ask which grades are being compared, whether the metric is Euclidean or not, whether a reverse or blade inverse is required, and whether the result should be a scalar or a lower-grade blade.

slides.title: Reciprocal Frames Extract Coordinates
slides.notes: Frame the reciprocal basis as a metric companion, not as a separate linear-algebra afterthought. In a skew frame, the reciprocal vectors become the probes that isolate coordinates through dot products satisfying the Kronecker-delta table for the chosen frame.

slides.title: Cross Product As Dual Area
slides.notes: Treat the familiar cross product as a bridge back to classical 3-D vector algebra. The geometric object is the oriented area blade, and the normal vector appears only after choosing the three-dimensional pseudoscalar and dualizing.

slides.title: Computation Should Audit Geometry
slides.notes: Tie the deck back to notebook practice. The implementation should compare contraction projection against a Gram solve, check residual orthogonality, inspect determinant collapse near dependence, and verify reciprocal-frame reconstruction instead of relying on axis-aligned coincidences.

slides.title: What Metric Products Add
slides.notes: Close by summarizing the new habit. A blade is no longer only an oriented span; with metric products it can be measured, compared, contracted, dualized, projected onto, rejected from, and used as a coordinate instrument.
